newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire expels U.N. workers, rebels target key areas.
newsitem.headline: Zaire expels U.N. workers, rebels target key areas.

text.p: Zaire has ordered the expulsion of 40 U.N. relief workers who withdrew from the eastern city of Kisangani last weekend, saying their departure triggered the alleged slaughter of Rwandan Hutus and displaced Zaireans.

A government statement broadcast by state radio late on Tuesday said 25,000 civilians had been slaughtered since mainly Tutsi rebels overran the Tingi Tingi refugee camp on Friday. There has been no independent confirmation of such killings.

A total of 57 foreign U.N. and non-governmental organisation relief workers pulled out of Kisangani last Saturday, saying degenerating security and harassment by local military authorities made it impossible for them to work.

"The precipitous departure of these humanitarian workers from the Tingi Tingi camp and the town of Kisangani...is considered by the government to be directly responsible for the slaughter which took place in less than 48 hours of 25,000 displaced persons and refugees," the government statement said.

"The government of the republic can no longer continue to condone the irresponsible behaviour of certain humanitarian agents...who have watched in silence during the massive killings committed by the Rwandan army in the refugee camps."

Zaire accuses the regular armies of Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of fomenting the almost five-month-old rebellion in eastern Zaire and of actively participating in fighting on Zairean soil. All three countries deny the allegations. Rebel forces in eastern Zaire are taking aim at the country's military and economic nerve centres with their armed campaign.
Moving with surprising ease, the Tutsi-led rebels have pushed towards the government army's operational base at Kisangani, Zaire's third city and diamond and gold trading centre.

A Defence Ministry official in the capital Kinshasa said the guerrillas gained more ground at the same time in the copper-producing Shaba Province to the south, taking the town of Kabalo with little resistance.
Kabalo is on the main railway line serving Shaba and 400 km (250 miles) south of the rail head at Kindu, which fell earlier.
"According to our information Kabalo was taken this morning," the defence official told Reuters.
He could not confirm rebel claims to have taken the town of Manono, 160 km (100 miles) south of Kabalo in the heart of the province. "We have no information on Manono at present," he said.
But he admitted Kindu had fallen to the guerrillas. Rebels had sent reinforcements into the town on Monday and the remaining Zairean troops there had fled, he said.
Zaire had until Monday maintained Kindu, 360 km (220 miles) north of Kabalo, was in government hands.

The capture of Kabalo and Manono would mark the rebels' first major advance in the southern province in weeks, and would place them within 500 km (310 miles) of the provincial capital Lubumbashi, the hub of Zaire's copper and cobalt industry.

The rebels who took up arms last October, initially to resist attempts to expel them to their ancestral homeland in Rwanda, have seized a vast stretch of eastern Zaire with seemingly little resistance by Zaire's mercenary-backed army.

Guerrilla leader Laurent Kabila says he is determined to end President Mobutu Sese Seko's 31-year rule. He has spurned international pressure for a ceasefire, insisting on direct negotiations with Mobutu. The ailing president is in France.
Kabila has proclaimed Kisangani as his next target, giving army commanders until March 13 to lay down their arms.
The rebels' push on Kabalo was their most important military move in Shaba since they seized the inland port of Kalemie, just inside the province, at the beginning of last month.
Some of the troops stationed there fled west through Kabalo, looting and at one stage hijacking a train on their way.
A senior director of the Sizarail rail company, which serves the entire south and central eastern region of Zaire with vital train links, said he had not yet heard of the capture of Kabalo.
He said that up until Monday the line was still open as far north as Kasongo, a station about 200 km (120 miles) from Kabalo.
With some despair, he said the spreading war was increasingly hampering the train company's ability to function.
As well as being an important link on the railway line, Kabalo has a power station, an airstrip and a small port on a navigable section of the broad Zaire river.
